text:
sam: thinking out loud — we need a clearer policy for bursts and backpressure. current behaviour is inconsistent: some keys get 429s immediately, others end up with queued work and slow 503 spikes. we should pick a principled approach.
anya: agreed. the core tradeoff is fast client-visible failure (429) vs system-level degradation (503) + slower responses. 429 is friendlier for clients that can retry. 503 signals infra trouble.
devin: +1. also important: per-key vs per-org. if a single key blasts traffic it should be limited without nailing org-wide throughput. token-bucket per-key + shared org reservoir seems right.
lucas: one idea: an "acceptance window" (e.g., 200ms) where bursts up to burst_size are accepted and handled with fast-path batching; after that we do early-drop 429s. avoids long tail queuing while letting short spikes pass.
anya: > acceptance window sounds good. need clear headers so clients know what happened. propose returning both Retry-After and X-RateLimit-* when we 429. for 503s include X-Service-Shedding: true so infra dashboards can filter them.
sam: example response patterns (proposal):
```
HTTP/1.1 429 Too Many Requests
Retry-After: 2
X-RateLimit-Limit: 50
X-RateLimit-Remaining: 0
X-RateLimit-Reset: 1710000000
```
or for infra saturation:
```
HTTP/1.1 503 Service Unavailable
X-Service-Shedding: accept-window-exhausted
```
devin: we should also emit a short token when we accept-but-queue (if we do any soft-queueing) so client can poll status rather than retry full request. rather than long blocking responses we could return 202 + queue-id. but that changes the API. not ideal.
lucas: agree 202 breaks flows. prefer small acceptance window + early drop instead of long queues. if a request is CPU-heavy (embedding large batch) we should pre-check and fail fast.
anya: metrics to add to console: ["acceptance_window_ms","accepted_burst_count","early_drop_count","service_shed_count","per_key_token_bucket_fill","org_reservoir_usage","queued_requests_count","retry_after_avg"] — show time-series and per-route breakdown. add a heatmap for keys generating most drops.
sam: UX idea for console: per-route toggle to prefer "client-failure-first" (429) vs "degrade-service" (503) for that route. default to client-first for public API endpoints, degrade-service for internal admin endpoints. that gives product teams control.
devin: implementation note: we should keep acceptance window in the ingress layer to avoid propagating expensive work into downstream pools. cheap check: if current_inflight_for_key + request_cost > bucket_capacity -> early drop. request_cost estimated from payload length / route profile.
lucas: drop strategy pseudocode:
```
if now - last_burst_start > acceptance_window_ms:
  reset burst_counter
if burst_counter < burst_limit:
  accept fast-path
else:
  if global_org_reservoir > 0:
    consume reservoir and accept
  else:
    return 429 with Retry-After
```

anya: one more: for long polls / streams we should treat them differently — they hold capacity for longer. streams should be subject to stricter admission (smaller per-key burst).
sam: backward compat: make headers opt-in via feature flag for 2 weeks so client teams can adopt parsing.
infra-bot: deploy request: canary policy-change -> ingress-rate-limiter v3.2 queued for 2m deploy window :rocket:
devin: action items: 1) add acceptance_window_ms config to ingress (sam) 2) instrument metrics listed above (anya) 3) add header spec and feature flag (devin) 4) console per-route toggle mockups (lucas). i'll open tickets.
sam: thanks — small follow-up: add a label to incidents when 503s exceed 5% of requests in a minute so oncall sees it as shedding, not upstream model errors.
anya: 👍 will add to alerts.
lucas: i'll sketch the console UX tomorrow and share.
sam: cool, locking in this approach: short acceptance window + early-drop 429s for client retries, explicit 503s for cluster-level shedding, per-key token buckets + org reservoir. we can iterate on queueing later if needed.
